result.summary: Pausanias lists statues and paintings on the Athenian Acropolis, then digresses into the history of Athens after Chaeronea: the Lamian War, Macedonian garrisons, and the tyranny of Lachares. It ends with Demetrius son of Antigonus fortifying the Museum hill.

scenes.title: Statues and paintings on the Acropolis
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes statues of Pericles, Xanthippus, Anacreon, Io and Callisto, and Attalus' paintings of battles. He also mentions Olympiodorus.

scenes.title: Chaeronea and the Lamian War
scenes.summary: After Chaeronea Philip crushes Greece. After Alexander's death Athens leads a revolt under Leosthenes, who dies, and the Macedonians garrison Athens' ports.

scenes.title: Cassander and Lachares
scenes.summary: Olympias is killed by Cassander, who installs Demetrius of Phalerum and then Lachares as tyrant. Demetrius son of Antigonus overthrows Lachares, who is killed in Boeotia for his wealth.
scenes.stakes: Athenian self-rule under tyrants and conquerors.

scenes.title: Demetrius fortifies the Museum
scenes.summary: Demetrius garrisons the Piraeus and fortifies the Museum hill, where Musaeus was said to be buried.

alias_notes.explanation: The Galatians, Celtic invaders defeated in Mysia.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias' judgment that Chaeronea began sorrows for all Greeks.

analysis.text: Art and monuments prompt a history of Athenian decline under Macedonian power, a recurring concern in Pausanias.
Pausanias, writing under Rome, treats Hellenistic conquests as the end of Greek liberty, focusing on Athens.

fun_facts.text: Attalus' paintings celebrated victories over Gauls, linking Athens to Pergamene royal propaganda.

language_notes.text: "Erotic poetry mainly" means Anacreon wrote chiefly love poetry; "in liquor" means drunk, as in his reputation for wine songs.
"Pourtrayed" is an old spelling of "portrayed"; a cubit is roughly 18 inches (about half a metre), so these paintings were small.
"Galati" are the Gauls (Celts) who invaded Asia Minor; Attalus, king of Pergamon, defeated them in Mysia.
Chæronea (338 BC) was where Philip of Macedon defeated Athens and Thebes, ending Greek independence.
"Generalissimo" means supreme commander of the combined forces.
The long walls linked Athens to its harbour at the Piræus; Munychia was a fortified hill above the harbour.
Musæus was a legendary early poet and seer, often linked with Orpheus.

context_notes.text: Io and Callisto were mortal women loved by Zeus and persecuted by Hera, his jealous wife.
After Alexander died in 323 BC, Athens led the Greek rising now called the Lamian War against Antipater.
Olympias was Alexander's mother; Cassander had her put to death in 316 BC.
Demetrius of Phalerum, a philosopher and orator, governed Athens for Cassander from 317 to 307 BC.

literary_notes.text: "A beginning of sorrows" presents a single defeat as the start of a long suffering, and "made slaves" figures lost freedom as slavery.
Lachares is condemned through a superlative, "most savage to men and most reckless to the gods", which sums up his tyranny.
Lachares's plunder of the sacred treasures makes him a rich target, and the wealth he stole brings about his death.
